title: Alfa Design Boss Says It: Get Rid of Giant Screens

body_markdown:
Monolithic slabs of pixels are everywhere in the car world. Screen size has become a major selling point in many market segments; Mercedes-Benz notably offers an optional 56-inch Hyperscreen[on some of its cars](https://www.hagerty.com/media/new-car-reviews/2022-mercedes-amg-eqs-review-fantastic-yet-fleeting/) . Alfa Romeo isn’t interested in joining this race. The company recognizes that you can’t sell a car without an infotainment system in the 2020s, but it plans to take a lower-tech approach to designing interiors in the coming years.


“Let’s get rid of the screens,” said Alfa Romeo design boss Alejandro Mesonero-Romanos in an interview with *[Autocar](https://www.autocar.co.uk/car-news/new-cars/alfa-romeo-design-boss-lets-get-rid-big-screens)* . “We are in search of emptiness. Screens are nice when you’re sitting in the car, but when you’re driving I’m not convinced. We’re in a kind of war of centimeters for the screens, and to me it doesn’t make any sense, because they become huge. They are designing the dashboard for you, basically.”


The head-turning[Cuorerosso concept](https://www.hagerty.com/media/design/alfa-romeos-cuorerosso-concept-is-a-welcome-sign-of-life/) (pictured) unveiled at the 2026 Paris auto show showcases this approach to design. It won’t reach production as-is, but it previews the design language that will shape Alfa Romeo’s next batch of models, including the next-generation Giulia and Stelvio. Its interior is a paradox, because it’s both highly futuristic and stunningly simple. The driver faces two round screens (a layout inspired by classic Alfa models) that merge into a single unit to let the driver focus on the road ahead.

For example, the car could activate the single-screen mode when it only needs to display basic information, like the speedometer and the tachometer. It could split the screens when the driver enters a navigation destination or needs to pull up a list of contacts.


The rest of the functions that are often lumped into the infotainment system screen can be accessed via the so-called Magma center console. It projects the information that the driver requests (like music options) onto a flat surface, and users can make a selection using either haptic touch controls or a physical dial. The idea is to make tech as subtle as possible: It’s there when you need it, and it’s not in the way when you don’t. This layout could allow Alfa Romeo to design cars without a touchscreen in the coming years.


What about keeping up with the competition? Mesonero-Romanos said that Alfa isn’t chasing the same buyers as its rivals.


“I’m aware that a big part of the public wants to have big screens, but then don’t buy an Alfa. Buy something else. I’m sure there are a lot of people out there who think like we do. There’s a lot of people that will be happy with this experience,” he concluded.


Alfa Romeo isn’t the only brand looking for an alternative to screens. Going low-tech is a growing trend, especially in the upper echelons of the automotive industry. Bugatti’s[upcoming Tourbillon](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/bugattis-next-chapter-the-tourbillon/) has only one screen, hidden in the top of the center console and revealed only when needed, giving the cabin a more streamlined look. Porsche went all-digital in[the updated 992.2-generation 911](https://www.hagerty.com/media/new-car-reviews/2025-porsche-911-carrera-gts-review-e-gads/) , but it replaced the touchscreen with a phone mount and the infotainment system with an app in[the new Mission S concept](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/mission-s-breaks-cover-and-points-porsche-to-a-new-path/) .


We’re glad to see some companies moving away from screen-dominant dashboards, and we’ll be even happier when the trend starts trickling down to more attainable models. Let us know what you think below.
